title: the Mandukya Karika (Gaudapada)
hook: a sparkler whirled in the dark draws circles that aren't there. the Karika's last section: the firebrand, held still

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mandukya Karika and the space inside a pot: smoke in one pot doesn't dirty the rest. When you poured out a cup, did you pause on the space left behind? Day one thousand two hundred forty-three.

A backyard after dark, and a kid with a sparkler. She swings it fast, and a ring of light hangs in the air. She swings it side to side and draws a glowing line. She writes her name, and for half a second the letters seem to float there. Then she stops, and holds it still. No ring. No letters. Just one small spitting point of light at the end of a wire. The circles never existed apart from that point. They were the point, moving. Gaudapada names the last section of the Mandukya Karika for nearly this picture, a burning stick from the fire, and today is our last day with him.
screen: `A SPARKLER IN THE DARK.` → `RINGS, LINES, A NAME.` → `HELD STILL: ONE POINT OF LIGHT.`

segments.voice: The Karika's last section is called Alatashanti, the quieting of the firebrand. An alata is a burning stick, a torch pulled from the fire. Gaudapada says: when a firebrand is whirled, it appears straight, or crooked, or circling. In the same way, when consciousness moves, it appears as the one who perceives and the things perceived. When the firebrand is still, it is free of all those shapes. When consciousness is still, it is free of them too. Then he presses the image further. When the torch is moving, the circles don't come into it from somewhere else. When it stops, they don't go off somewhere else. And they don't sink back inside it either. They were never things on their own. That's his point about the world of experience: on his reading, it isn't a second thing standing apart from consciousness. It's how consciousness appears when it moves. Gaudapada knows this is hard to hear. In this same section he speaks of a teaching that is deep and hard to see, and at the very end he offers a salute to it, bowing as well as he is able. So the Karika ends not with an argument but with a bow. Across these days we've met his waking, dream and sleep, the rope, no birth, the ocean and the blade of grass, the pots, and now the torch. Advaita teachers count him as an early voice of their lineage, and tradition says he taught the teacher of Shankara. Other schools of Vedanta read the world as more fully real, and say so with their own arguments.
screen: `ALATA: A BURNING STICK.` · `WHIRLED, IT DRAWS SHAPES.` · `THE SHAPES COME FROM NOWHERE ELSE.` · `THE KARIKA ENDS WITH A BOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let the firebrand slow down. Sit, and feel the breath come and go. Notice the mind's motion: plans, pictures, bits of conversation, each one a shape the torch draws as it swings. Don't try to stop them. Just watch them form and fade. Between them, look for a moment when the swinging slows, and there's simply awareness, not drawing anything. Rest there as long as it lasts. When the shapes start again, watch again. If you pray, you can end by bowing your head, the way the Karika ends. The bell holds the time.
The Mandukya Karika. Gaudapada's verses on the Mandukya Upanishad, which end with a torch held still and a bow to a truth he calls deep and hard to see. Today's word.

Your line: the Mandukya Karika, Gaudapada. Today, when your mind starts circling one worry, picture the torch, and let it slow for one breath. Tomorrow the path turns to the Vedas themselves. Day one thousand two hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta, the Mandukya Upanishad is often studied together with Gaudapada's Karika and Shankara's commentary on both, and the firebrand image is used by teachers to point to consciousness behind the movement of the mind.

a bow, as well as he is able

fork.setup: you've spent a whole book arguing that the world is consciousness in motion. you reach the last verse. what do you do?
options: sum up the argument one more time.
bow to the truth you've been pointing at.
fork.reveal: Gaudapada ends with a salute: he bows, as well as he is able, to a teaching he calls deep and hard to see.

original.note: Sanskrit: the quieting of the firebrand, from alata, a burning stick, and shanti, peace. The name of the Karika's last section.

trapdoor: what you thought: the firebrand is just a pretty picture.
what it means: for Gaudapada, the world of experience is consciousness appearing as it moves, like rings drawn by a whirled torch.
what a scholar hears: Mandukya Karika 4.47–4.52, the alata image of vibrating consciousness, and the closing salute in 4.100.

sources.ref: Mandukya Karika 4.47–4.52 (the firebrand whirled appears straight or crooked; consciousness vibrating appears as perceiver and perceived; the shapes neither come from elsewhere, go elsewhere, nor enter into it)
Mandukya Karika 4.100 (the state deep and hard to see; the salute offered as well as one is able)

notes: Mandukya Karika 4.47–4.52 and 4.100 paraphrased; no public-domain translation on the validator list. Confirm the paraphrase of 4.49–4.50 (the appearances neither come from elsewhere, nor go elsewhere, nor enter it).
'Tradition says he taught the teacher of Shankara' (Gaudapada as Govinda's teacher, Govinda as Shankara's) is stated as tradition, not history. Confirm wording.
The teach's recap follows days 1238–1242 (the states, the rope, ajati, the ocean and the cup, the pots).
The sparkler is a modern hook; Gaudapada's image is a firebrand (alata). Original alatashanti: confirm Devanagari and pronunciation.

Editor: the hook no longer says the Karika 'closes' with the firebrand (it is the last section's image, 4.47–4.52; the close is the salute in 4.100); recap corrected from 'the cup' to 'the blade of grass' to match day 1241.
